items.detail: Closed, not expanded. The TSA combination lock and the compression pads are built in, and it ships with a drawstring laundry bag — so that's one thing off the list. Do NOT use the expansion zipper — an expanded case is over most carriers' checked dimensions and the Z165 luggage space is not generous.

At 72 cm tall it is over Korean Air's 55 × 40 × 20 cm cabin size on paper, but it's soft and compresses; the binding limit is the 10 kg you're allowed across the carry-on and personal item together. Cinch the compression straps and don't let it look like a trekking pack at the gate.

20–26 litres is the sweet spot — big enough for a poncho, a layer, water and snacks at Disney, small enough to pass the park's bag screening and to fold into the Talon for base camp. Anything over 30 L duplicates the Talon and costs you cabin weight. Still to pick which one comes. It is the bag for park days and for the EBC eco-bus — the Talon stays at the hotel on Disney days.

See the picks above. Worn on the front and zipped in every crowd. Shanghai is where Sandra got scammed. Worn crossbody, and the one bag that never leaves you — including on the coasters, where a shoulder bag is a problem.
Under 50 g and it decides whether you pay excess in Lhasa. Weigh the Away before every flight, not just at home.
Long johns, heavy socks, base layer, hat, gloves, warmers, wipes. At Shigatse you lift one cube out of the Away into the Talon and you're packed for base camp.
Osprey doesn't include one with the Talon 44. It is less about rain than about plateau dust and the pack riding on a roof rack for 340 km.
Reclaims a surprising amount of space in a 44 L pack that has to hold a night's kit.
Plateau dust gets into everything. Also keeps electronics dry on the passes.
The Away has its own TSA lock; the Talon has nothing. The soft sleeper cabin locks, but the bags in it don't.
Nineteen days out of one bag means sink washing at least twice. The Away's own laundry bag holds the dirty half.
Domestic Chinese flights check bags against your ticket at the carousel.

Z165 has no paper ticket: you board on the passport. Also your Disney admission, every hotel check-in, and station security. Lives in the sling, never the pack: it is the Z165 boarding pass, the Tibet permit check and your real-name Disney ticket, so it comes out several times a day.
Checked to board the train and again at road checkpoints. Photograph it the moment James delivers it.

FAFD77, GBDPCB, JP5E6A, AOT-BJ-James-50674. Paper survives a dead phone. Flights, hotels, the tour receipt and the day-by-day on paper — the copy that still works with a dead phone behind the firewall.
On the phone in a folder that works with no signal, plus emailed to yourself.
One card lives in the Talon instead, so a lost sling isn't a lost trip. Foreign cards still fail at plenty of Chinese terminals.
ATMs thin out past Shigatse and there are none at base camp. Small notes.
A few hundred RMB across the eight days, in cash, in an envelope, separate from your spending money.
Two or three hundred, buried in the checked bag, kept separately from everything else.
Permits, and whatever else asks.
On paper. The number you need is the one you can't look up.
James +86 177 2640 4023; Chengdu consulate +86 28 8558 3992 (nearest post to Tibet); Shanghai +86 21 6433 6880; Overseas Citizens Services +1 202 501 4444.
Hand it to the taxi driver. Screenshot each one as well.
At 1.5 L and 2.4 in deep it doubles as the flat pouch for the passport and permit on the two transit days where losing them ends the trip. The Waistpack does the job the rest of the time.
Keep one clean and unworn for the base camp night.
You sleep in these at EBC. Wool, not cotton.
The layer you'll live in for a week.
Lives in the carry-on so it's never lost and never counted: Lhasa evenings, every pass stop, and under the shell at base camp.
Wear it on the plane. Wind at the passes is the real problem, not rain, and it covers Xi'an showers too.
Pack small, worth their weight standing around at 5,200 m.
Softshell for the plateau days, lighter for Lhasa.
For the cities, where technical clothing looks odd.
Quick-dry ones earn their place — you'll do sink laundry.
Five nights in Shanghai with dinners you haven't planned yet.
Two pairs live in the Talon so a delayed bag isn't a crisis. Cotton stays wet; merino or synthetic.
Wool or synthetic, no cotton. Also the Disney answer: a dry pair in the day bag on a 20,000-step day is the difference between finishing the evening and not.
One dry pair reserved for sleeping. Cold feet keep you awake all night.
You lose most of your heat here and you'll sleep in it at base camp.
Clipped to the outside of the daypack. The plateau sun is relentless at midday even when the air is cold. Plateau sun at 5,000 m and a full day queueing in Shanghai are the same problem.
One in the sling, one in the Away. Sun on the neck, dust on the roads, wind on the face — the most useful small thing you'll carry.
Liners let you work a camera without bare hands at 21 °F (−6 °C).
On you, spare pair in the Away. Glare off snow at 5,200 m is genuinely damaging.
In the carry-on, because the first night you need it is on the train, thirty hours before you next see the Away. Four-berth cabin with strangers, then a twin room with Jeff.
City hotel pools. Weighs nothing.
72 °F (22 °C) days, 59 °F (15 °C) nights. The hardshell also does this job if you'd rather save the space. Doubles as the park layer — something you can take off at midday and stuff in the day bag.
Long trousers, covered shoulders, hat off indoors. Potala, Jokhang, Sera and Tashilhunpo are all working religious sites.
Cheaper than buying one in the park, and Roaring Rapids will genuinely soak you.

Wear them on the plane. Never check the shoes you can't replace, and they're the heaviest single thing you own. Worn in before you fly. New boots on the plateau is how a trip gets ruined in the first two days, and there is no fixing it once you are up there.

The Xi'an wall and several 20,000-step days at Disney. Rotating between these and the boots is the best thing you can do for your feet. The second pair matters on the park days: alternating shoes across three 20,000-step days is worth more than any insole.

Don't fly a pair of rubber slides across the Pacific — buy them in Xi'an on day one; see "Buy it in China". Then they live in the Talon, because you need them in the train corridor before you ever open the Away. Train corridor, the tent camp and any shared shower. Cheap to pick up in Xi'an if you would rather not pack them.
Cheap insurance against cold feet on the plateau.
Start it on the schedule they give you, not when you feel bad — which means it has to be on you, not in the hold.
Tiny, cheap, and turns "I feel off" into a number you can act on.
A working supply in the Talon, the rest of the box in the Away. Altitude headache is near-universal.
Nausea and appetite loss are the most common complaints at base camp.
Seven hours to Shigatse and 340 km over three passes above 5,000 m. You need these in the van, not in the pack in the boot.
Sandra lost four days in Xi'an to food poisoning. Assume it will happen once, and keep two sachets in the sling.
You need three to four litres a day up there and plain water won't keep up.
The full course in the Talon, a duplicate set in the Away, and a copy of the prescription in both.
The dry plateau air shreds throats within a couple of days.
Nosebleeds at altitude are routine and unpleasant in a shared room.

The big tube is over 100 ml so it has to go in the Away; carry a 50 ml one in the sling. UV at 5,200 m burns skin you didn't know was exposed — under the chin, inside the nose, ears. Large tube checked, small tube on you. The park days need it as much as the plateau does.
One in the sling, the spare in the Away. You will lose one, and cracked lips at altitude take the whole trip to heal.
Dust, wind and dry air, all at once.
In the day bag, not the hotel. Before the hot spot becomes a blister. In your pocket, not the hotel room — a hotspot at 11:00 is a blister by 14:00 either at base camp or in a queue.
Nothing elaborate. The guide carries a kit too.
One in the sling, one in the daypack, one in the Talon, one in a coat pocket.
Twelve hours of time change on the way out. Do not take a sleeping pill at altitude, though.
Sandra's diet in China ran to noodles, rice and pork, and she felt the gap.
A travel set in the Talon for the train, the full one in the Away. Brush with bottled water. Every time.
Big tub checked, a small tube in the sling. The plateau is bone dry and your hands will crack.
This is your shower on 7 October.

Pocket-level, always. Squat toilets rarely supply paper, and base camp has pit toilets. Sandra repeats this more than any other tip. Carry a packet at all times: public toilets rarely supply paper. Restock in bulk once you are there rather than flying a month's worth in.
The camp provides nothing.
Hotels supply these; camps don't. Travel sizes only — full-size bottles are cheap and everywhere once you land.
Clippers in the checked bag — they will be taken off you at security otherwise.
Bring the glasses even if you never wear them — dust and dry air make lenses miserable above 4,000 m.
Road dust on the plateau, and still normal in Chinese cities.
Pit toilets, no lighting, no supplies. In a pocket, not in a bag in the tent. A part-roll in a pocket. There is no paper at the base camp toilets and none on most of the drive.
A second handset covers theft, loss, and a Chinese SIM in one device. Keep them in different bags. Worth bringing your old handset as a backup too — it is your ticket, your wallet and your only map.

Bought in Xi'an, not brought — your American one is not legal on the Lhasa–Shanghai flight; see "Buy it in China". It then lives in the Talon: carry-on only, never checked, because lithium in the hold is banned outright in China. BUY THIS IN XI'AN, do not fly one in. China requires a moulded 3C mark that no US-market battery carries, lithium cannot go in the hold, and an uncertified pack is confiscated at Lhasa on the way to Shanghai. Assume no reliable power on the Z165, none at the tent camp, and a full day off-charger at the park.
Cables fail. Bring the spare.
One in the Talon, one in the Away. Chinese sockets vary by building age.
There is no lighting at the base camp toilets. A phone torch works until the phone dies. With spare batteries — easy to pick up there rather than pack.
Cold flattens camera batteries — spares in an inside pocket, and in your sleeping bag overnight. If you'd rather have it to hand all day, that's the argument for the Peak Design sling.
Thirty hours in a four-berth cabin, then a thin-walled tent camp.
Wired ones don't need charging on a thirty-hour train.
Avoid a printed guidebook to Tibet — political content gets confiscated at checkpoints. Download it instead.
For the base camp sunrise, when your phone may be flat.

Sandra credits a Chinese SIM three separate times with saving her trip — but that advice has inverted since 2017. A local SIM now sits inside the firewall and would kill WhatsApp, which is how James reaches you. Install a travel eSIM at home instead: it routes through a foreign carrier, so WhatsApp, mail and maps just work. A local SIM is worth it only for rural Tibet coverage, and only if the guide arranges it. Installed BEFORE you fly — it cannot be downloaded from inside the firewall. It is also what keeps you connected through a full park day, when the ticket, the queue times and the wallet are all on the phone.
For the same reason.
The camp quilts are heavy and warm but not always clean. The liner adds a few degrees too, and weighs almost nothing.

Optional; the camp quilts do work. But carrying your own from Atlanta costs another 1.5 kg, and Lhasa rents them by the day. James can arrange it with the tour. Rated to about −10 °C. Rent it in Lhasa rather than carrying one across three cities — but it is a real decision, so it stays on the list.

Not currently on your list, and worth a thought for the walk in at base camp. Rented alongside the sleeping bag rather than checked from Atlanta. Rent in Lhasa. Only worth it if you intend to walk beyond the base camp marker.

Your packable puffy is not enough at 21 °F (−6 °C) with wind, and a real parka is 1.5–2 kg of a 14.5 kg budget. The rental shops around Barkhor exist for exactly this trade. The single easiest kilo to save. Rent or buy around Barkhor in Lhasa. Cheaper and warmer than anything you would pack, and you hand it back.
Two in the boots, two in the gloves, two in the sleeping bag. Cheap, weightless, transformative.

Appetite collapses at altitude. Bring things you'll eat when you don't want to eat — and pack them where you can reach them, not in the Away. One stock, four jobs: thirty hours on the Z165, the drive days, the tent night where dinner is basic and early, and the park, where a queue is a bad place to be hungry. Buy the bulk of it in Xi'an.
Hot water is available almost everywhere in China.
Given the hot water, a real quality-of-life item.
Optional, but station chopsticks are sanitised and reused.
A backup for the plateau, where buying bottled water gets harder and pricier.
There are refill points, and you will drink more than you expect on a warm day. A wide-mouth one doubles as a hot-water bottle in the tent, filled from the camp thermos.
Every carriage has a boiling-water dispenser and this is how everyone eats and drinks on Chinese trains. Buy it in Xi'an before you board rather than carrying one from home.

Postcards of Atlanta, pins, small candy — a few in the Talon for the train, the rest in the Away. Sandra handed out NYC postcards and says it landed every single time. Also the answer to the soft-sleeper cabin: something small to hand over goes a long way across thirty hours and no shared language.
Many monasteries charge for photography and some ban it outright. Ask first, always.
Landing cards, hotel names, and the phone numbers you'll need when the phone is dead.
Repairs a bag strap, a boot, a tent zip.
Clip it to the outside of the pack. The berths are flat but short.
